residency, but does not directly relate to his time at CERN, nor to the crisis in 

confidence he experienced there. 

In contrast, the second international Collide@CERN winner Bill Fontana’s 

carefully planned artwork was produced in its entirety at CERN. In his sound piece, The 

Universe of Sound, the LHC was his main inspiration. Fontana approached the LHC as 

an object, recording its mechanical sounds and creating a rhythmic soundtrack for 

CERN. The mechanical rhythm repeats and becomes increasingly intense. The piece was 

released on YouTube in autumn 2013, enabling commenters to share their opinions. One 

commenter wrote:  

 

Love science, love CERN, but this video is disappointing. 
We hear some strange sounds but do not get explanations of what they are. 
We are told an artist is performing some kind of experiment, but we do not 
get a full explanation or see any results. This is no way to promote science. 
If those of us who already love science and know something about it do 
not understand this, then the average layman will be left completely put-off 
by such meaningless confusing nonsense.63 
 
 

Another YouTube user is less patient, stating: “What a surprise, a pretentious lame idea 

from the art world.”64 These kinds of anonymous reactions are of course easy to express 

on a medium such as YouTube, and with only 1,680 views the interest was not big. 

Nevertheless, the medium of YouTube fits Arts@CERN’s interactive, social media-

aware, interdisciplinary mode. Furthermore, as none of the Collide@CERN art was 

exhibited, it is one of the few ways to understand how the public reacted to the artworks. 

Fontana is still working with the sounds he collected from CERN, but the LHC 

recording remains his main output from his residency.

5.6 Benefit to artists 

As each artist thanked CERN for the residency opportunity, they reflected on what they 

had gained from the interaction. They all gratefully acknowledged the chance to 

collaborate in an interesting space and with interesting people. Making contact with the

always important. While some confidence might have been lost along the way, the

who benefit from this. Thus, a hierarchy is established. By controlling which artists are 

invited to CERN, the organisation might cut itself off from some truly fascinating 

interventions. Nevertheless, for those who do win the various competitions, the benefits 

of being an artist at CERN have, on a whole, never been bigger.   

 

5.7 Conclusion 

In this chapter I have explored the Collide@CERN artists, asking who they are, what 

experiences they have had at the organisation, what the work they made there means, 

and what benefits they gained from the residency. I have found that their time at CERN 

is not without conflict, but that it is usually a positive experience. Some artists created 

art as a direct consequence of spending time at CERN, and all of the winners gained 

access to networks, prizes, recognition and some financial stability post-CERN. While 



! 221!

most of the artists struggled with an inferiority complex in their interactions with 

scientists, many created warm working relationships with their science partners despite 

this.83 Selected from a pool of over 300 applicants, the artists were already filtered by 

CERN and found to be suitable matches for the organisation’s goals. Furthermore they 

(and other CERN artists) usually mirrored the demographic makeup of CERN staff in 

terms of their nationalities, their gender and the career stage that they were in. In the 

artists’ post-residency relationships with CERN they may also continue to benefit from 

the organisation’s networks. Having access to CERN gives individual artists access to 

certain networks and benefits. But in the controlled cultural atmosphere of the cultural 

board and residency application system, artists who are not invited to work with the 

organisation have little chance of visiting the site. While they may share a passion for 

science, these artists can now be excluded from CERN. So what is it like for the artist 

who does have CERN as a studio today? Under contract, freedom may be compromised, 

but there are also new opportunities, networks and benefits to explore. Furthermore, in a 

time where some art residencies ask artists to pay a fee, Collide@CERN treats artists as 

professionals.84 Gaining knowledge, friendships, funding and access to networks, 

Collide@CERN artists are as celebrated by the organisation as the organisation is 

celebrated by them.

CONCLUSION 

Boundary Breakers? Artists at CERN. 

 

In this thesis I asked why CERN is investing its resources in a structured art programme 

now. The answers presented reveal the institutional structure of SciArt through the case 

study of CERN. CERN has always had an active PR office, and branding and image 

have become integral to how it operates as a globally recognised organisation. CERN’s 

goal of legitimising its work as part of its survival strategy remains, and PR is crucial to 

sustaining this. CERN’s PR strategy has changed over the decades, but has only very 

recently included the arts and artists. This thesis has, for the first time, questioned these 

SciArt structures as features of promotional culture in science. In this conclusion I 

discuss the key findings that have been revealed from this analysis. I reflect on my 

methodology, revisit the key findings of the individual chapters, explore how this project 

expands various literatures, and discuss key themes. 

 

Reflections on methodology  

This thesis utilised interviews, archival research, site visits, art historical approaches, 

and theories of gender and cultural capital as part of its methodological framework. I 

used an inductive approach to interpret this data. This approach proved to be successful 

because it allowed me to understand the patterns and relationships between the 

economic, institutional and cultural factors that have created an art project at CERN 

today. While the textual sources and interviews provided rich contextual evidence to 

support the claims made in this thesis, as in all research, there are limitations regarding 

the researcher’s interpretations of the data. Nevertheless, using both primary and 

secondary data has provided a broad and unique understanding of arts at CERN, and of 

how scientific institutions such as CERN shape and control SciArt. 

 

Reflections on chapters 

The first chapter, ‘Image’, explored the historical use of PR and branding at CERN. I 

provided a scholarly investigation of CERN’s PR office, drawing on archival material 

and interviews. I used the case study of the ‘Higgs Boson Blues’ to find out how 



! 223!

CERN’s history of PR has informed its current Communication Group. I examined this 

through a close reading of the song’s lyrics. I also interviewed the current head of the PR 

office, James Gillies, and found that CERN as a rule differentiates between art and 

popular culture (although the exceptions to this reveals insight into other public 

engagement goals), and that it choses what it has time to engage with. I also explored the 

controversial issues that surround the organisation, in particular questions of gender and 

diversity, conspiracy theories, and financial pressures. Understanding these difficult 

topics explain why CERN needs PR today. The thesis shows that the Communication 

Group’s main task is to maintain CERN’s identity. But in the new post-Internet media 

landscape, the nature of PR is changing. I argue that art and artists are part of this change 

in PR at CERN, and that while they have agency, they do not have control over these 

structures. 

In the second chapter, ‘Contracted’, I explored SciArt and found that it lends 

itself to the goals of CERN’s PR office. Through examining the field of SciArt, and 

exploring how other physics laboratories have used the arts in the past, I argued that the 

institutional nature of this new genre is perfectly suited to CERN’s needs. I traced the 

start of SciArt back to the Wellcome Trust’s initiative in the ‘90s, and showed how, ever 

since, the field has always been tied to institutions and hierarchical structures. This is the 

first critical examination of the field and history of SciArt, in contrast to most SciArt 

literature that celebrates or explains the field. I argue that SciArt, like any genre of art, 

should be carefully examined, and that this includes investigating the financial and 

institutional factors that created it.  

The third chapter, ‘Pasts’, presented the history of CERN art. Drawing on 

archival research, interviews, visits to CERN and art historical analysis, I introduce the 

artworks at the organisation. This is the first time the organisation’s visual culture has 

been explored. I show how CERN’s art history is eclectic and varied, comparing works 

that celebrate the organisation with pieces that engage in controversial topics. Drawing 

on my work about the history of PR at CERN, I show how the organisation employs 

silencing strategies in cases of controversial art. This provides an important framework 

for understanding how contemporary artists are chosen for the new art residency, and 

how they might experience their time at CERN. The chapter also argues that CERN has 



! 224!

always inspired artists, and that it is only now that the organisation seeks to culturally 

capitalise on this creativity, and thus improve its image to prove its legitimacy and 

secure funding.  

In the fourth chapter, ‘Control’, I explore why CERN is seeking to culturally 

capitalise on art and artists since 2011. I explore the origin of Arts@CERN, examining 

the people and financial support that created the project. For this, I analysed the 

economic and historical factors behind the origins of the scheme. I also used historical 

methods to explore E.A.T. and CAVS, comparing these two early science and art 

schemes with Arts@CERN. CERN is unique in significant ways, but comparing its art 

programme to E.A.T. and CAVS shows how CERN has chosen to shape Arts@CERN 

today. The chapter also presents a close textual analysis of CERN’s new cultural policy, 

showing how the rhetoric of this text underlines the organisation’s attitude to the arts 

and to artists. 

In the final chapter, ‘Artists’, I focused on the artists’ experiences at CERN 

today. I explored what type of artists succeed in the new Collide@CERN residency 

competition in terms of demography, stage of career and art medium. I looked at the 

experiences they had whilst at CERN, and the outcomes they produced (lectures, 

interventions, art and networks). I analysed the artists’ statements about confidence and 

creativity whilst at CERN, showing how there was an inferiority complex at work in 

many cases. I argued that although the artists gained some funding, networks, 

opportunities and friendship from the exchange, it was CERN that gained most. Having 

explored how CERN’s strong culture of PR has worked since the start of the 

organisation, and how the office did not culturally capitalise on the many artistic 

projects that took place before Arts@CERN, we can see why, in a time of intense 

reputational and financial pressures, the Communication Group sought to capitalise on 

this free opportunity. CERN has not had any expenses throughout Arts@CERN, as the 

money comes from external donors. In this context I argue that although Arts@CERN 

provides genuine creative ‘collisions’ between artists and scientists, it is also a genuine 

PR opportunity. The latter is what structures both the organisation’s cultural policy and 

attitude towards the arts, and based on my research I believe that CERN’s own interests 

will always be privileged over those of individual artists. This questions the common 



! 225!

notion that artists should be free to be creative, showing how both SciArt and 

Arts@CERN use the stereotypes surrounding artists for their own gains. These themes 

and my findings are discussed in detail below. 

 

Reflections on literature  

In this thesis I utilised several fields of scholarship, bringing them together in new ways 

from an art historical perspective. While interdisciplinary research can be challenging, it 

can also strengthen a project. Drawing on art history, science history, science 

communication studies, branding theory, sociology, anthropology, social science and 

gender studies, I have situated CERN in an interdisciplinary and complex reality (these 

literatures are discussed and referenced in the literature review part of the introduction). 

Most scholarship on CERN has focused on its scientific work and its machines. Utilising 

interdisciplinary literatures, I have shown how CERN is not only about science; it is also 

a cultural, economic and political space.  

Each separate field of scholarship has provided rich context to this study of 

SciArt at CERN, and in turn this project has located some limitations in the individual 

scholarly fields, and sought to fill those gaps. Within art history, there are very few 

scholars who explore science. Most of those who do, engage with scientific theory or 

discoveries. In contrast, this thesis explores the visual culture of a scientific institution, 

drawing on art historical methodology. In the history of science, many scholars have 

explored the culture of science, but there has been little engagement with the visual 

culture of scientific organisations. This thesis explores the scientific history of CERN, 

but focuses on the history of PR and art at the organisation, rather than on scientific 

theories or machines. In science communication studies we have been shown evidence 

for the relationship between PR and science. This thesis expands this relationship to 

include artists, and shows how they are also part of the science communication network 

of contemporary science. Sociologists and anthropologists have long been interested in 

how scientists work. In this thesis I show how artists, as both non-scientists and 

professionals, experience a scientific organisation. I have explored how this clash of 

cultures functions as useful PR for CERN, and is at times complicated for the 

individuals involved. Gender studies and feminist science theory have explored the lack 



! 226!

of women in science, the forgotten women of the past, and the theoretical implications 

of inequality. In this thesis, I have shown that there is not only a lack of women at 

CERN, but also a lack of women in SciArt and Arts@CERN. I have argued that there 

needs to be a dedicated analysis of inequality in SciArt, and that the lack of diversity in 

Arts@CERN and Ars Electronica could start that conversation. I have also drawn on 

Bordieu’s ideas about cultural capital, expanding this to explore scientific capital and 

artistic capital at CERN. Thus, the project draws on several vast literatures, addressing 

limitations in these fields, and filling some gaps. Likewise, this work should be of 

interest to art historians who work on science, science historians, science communication 

scholars, sociologists and anthropologists of science, economists who explore science or 

art, and scholars who work on theories relating to science and art.  

 

Key findings 

This study is unique in its focus on the institutional history of SciArt. Artists experience 

CERN as non-scientists and creative observers, led through a series of initiation 

processes in order to produce desired outcomes for the organisation. These outcomes 

(whether art works, interventions, debate or other forms of cultural capital) benefit the 

organisation more than it does the individual scientists or artists involved in the 

programme. In the mid-‘90s, the pioneering SciArt programme initiated by the 

Wellcome Trust found that artists stood to gain more than scientists from collaboration.1 

In this thesis the focus has been redirected towards the institutional nature of the 

collaboration, the entity that is profiting most from SciArt. This is not to say that artists 

and scientists get nothing from the CERN art programme, but they are neither the 

catalysts nor main beneficiaries of its structure.  

A key issue explored in this thesis concerns how artists, in the course of their 

interaction with CERN, function both as non-scientists and professionals who lend their 

expertise to ‘sell’ CERN’s brand. Some artists have experiences of CERN that are 

similar to other non-scientist groups, not fully accessing the inner workings of the 

organisation, either because they do not wish to, or because they are not invited to. They

organisation. CERN’s new cultural board and cultural policy enables the organisation to 

choose which artists work on the site, and whom they work with. Arts@CERN also

Giving an account of this organic and often messy process shows the many faces of 

CERN. From sculptures to dystopian fiction, from the neighbours’ opinions to feminist 

pop, the organisation has inspired a large output of culture that it now seeks to capitalise 

on. But instead of engaging with these artworks, CERN is focused on SciArt. In the 

creation of the residency competition, the cultural board and the cultural policy in 2011, 

control over cultural activities at CERN is now vested in a small group of experts. It 

mirrors the concentration of power in scientific institutions, and indeed is parallel to 

CERN’s own history as it emerges as an influential scientific diplomat (exemplified by 

its presence at Davos and in the UN).3  

While SciArt collaborations serve institutional agendas, of course artists can also 

benefit from these arrangements. Residencies can offer some security for artists, as a 

source of income. Institutional reviews of SciArt usually focus on what the artist and 

scientist can get from the exchange.4 This thesis showed that the benefits for individual 

artists or scientists are less observable than those gained by CERN. In the service of 

science, the artist becomes a smaller figure in a grander plan of survival and legitimacy 

for the individual host institution. In the case of CERN, the artist brings the elusive blue-

sky qualities needed to make a case for mystery and awe, and functions as part of the 

organisation’s long-term survival strategy by promoting a positive message. While the 

artists gain funding and networks from this interaction, it is CERN that has gained most 

from the collaboration, in particular new networks, funding and media attention. Studies 

of SciArt have until now focused on individuals rather than institutional structures.

how institutions benefit from SciArt and what social, economic and political structures 

form as a consequence. Future studies could ask similar questions of the Wellcome

A further significant finding of this thesis centres on the outcomes of the art 

programme at CERN today. The focus of Arts@CERN is on collaboration and 

discussion, rather than on making art. There is no expectation that the artist will produce 

an artwork by the end of their residency. Nevertheless, as this thesis shows, CERN often 

holds artists to account after their residencies finish. The job of the artist can sometimes 

be to deepen the mystery of their host institution. In the current art programme at CERN, 

the creative participants have in part been brought in to do this job. In some cases, the 

direction established by their time at CERN continues to be followed after the residency 

ends (Peters, Jobin, Ikeda, Fontana). Others are not directly inspired by CERN in their 

post-residency existence (von Bismark, visiting and shortlisted artist), yet regardless the 

organisation claims a positive outcome. The promise of future benefits outlasting the 

actual residency is similar to that of the CERN Knowledge Transfer Group, the office 

that works on disseminating knowledge about the organisation’s future scientific spin-

offs. Promising future outcomes, whether creative or scientific, is one way for the 

organisation to secure its future funding and existence.  

 To this end, artists are coopted to CERN’s branding strategy. Post-Higgs era 

CERN continues its work in the public sphere, often with the help of science museums, 

journalists, celebrities and individuals such as Ariane Koek. The exhibition Collider at 

the Science Museum is one example, as are CERN’s many public Twitter accounts, 

public speakers such as Brian Cox, and visiting celebrities such as Will.i.am. There was 

already SciArt activity at CERN prior to Ariane Koek’s arrival there, but it was not 

coordinated or publicised in a way that would reach people beyond the high-energy 

physics community and, more importantly, funders. Today, CERN has made culture part 

of its PR through utilising SciArt as public engagement. As an organisation dependent 

on public funding and being seen as legitimate, PR is part of its survival strategy. It is 

not surprising that CERN wants its SciArt to function as PR, and place their artists under 

contract. However, since CERN was founded 1954 it has wrestled with critics and 

conspiracy theories that have endangered its reputation, and thereby its survival. CERN 



! 230!

cannot control all these external interpretations of itself. But, as we have seen, it can 

distribute its message through careful selection of artists. In the past, this was not done, 

and many artists produced conspiracy theories because the laboratory captured their 

imagination. Today, through the Arts@CERN structure, CERN can harness positive 

messages from handpicked artists, and exclude artists who do not comply with the 

organisation’s narrative. Thus, CERN is using cultural capital to communicate its 

importance to the outside world. Whether this strategy is beneficial or not will depend 

on how the public and funders view CERN in the future. After discovering the 

anticipated Higgs boson, it is not clear what happens next for CERN. In a situation based 

on public opinion and changing factors, the art programme at CERN is not necessarily 

safe from being cut in the future. But for now, Koek has shown that artists can be used 

in the organisation’s branding strategy through media coverage, and through the 

Collide@CERN initiated projects, that disseminate knowledge about CERN in the art 

world. 

Of the SciArt inspired by CERN, or catalysed by Arts@CERN, most of it 

revolves around what the artist has learned from science, rather than the other way 

around. While the goal of Arts@CERN is to facilitate an equal exchange of outputs, this 

outcome is in line with the rest of the SciArt world. The 2009 review of the Wellcome 

Trust’s SciArt initiative found that in most projects involving artists and scientists, the 

scientific capital had not increased in line with cultural, economic, aesthetic, social, 

personal, innovative or educational capital.5 While the initiative was found to have had 

“high impact”, it was thus unbalanced between the two main groups. At CERN, this was 

particularly evident when it comes to dance and choreography, where each of the 

choreographers involved has cast the dancer in the role of particle, and in photography, 

where most concentrate on the empty spaces and corridors of the site. Isabelle Stengers 

has argued that the content of the sciences is intrinsically linked to the ideologies of its 

images.6 At CERN, some artists are a part of the trend within SciArt that embraces the 

mysticism of non-applied physics. This mysticism is connected to what Sharon Traweek 

has described as pride in not engaging with applied science within the high-energy

would not have achieved without the project. The art, while part of these larger 

outcomes, was not the main focus for Arts@CERN. 

These findings reveal an institution that is both welcoming and excluding to 

laypeople. While some artists move from a layperson position to becoming an accepted 

colleague at CERN (Peters in particular), the hope of their boundary-breaking qualities 

as expressed in the CERN cultural policy does not always manifest itself. In the context 

of a broader commercialised art and science market, this poses the question of the effects 

of contracts like Collide@CERN upon the creative process of artists. The new art 

programme has changed the way in which artists respond to CERN. Now more 

streamlined, some of the spontaneous character of artists’ visits has been lost. 

Arts@CERN has altered some hierarchies by placing the winning artist and scientists 

together. But it has created others, such as a selection process and the privileging of 

specific types of art over others.  

As explored in this thesis, the artists may also find themselves contracted to a 

theme or ideology. Some freedom is lost in the exchange between the individual and the 

institution. On the other hand, the experiences of the artists pre- and post-Arts@CERN 

reveal how much the professions of art and science have in common. The individuals 

who have been part of the CERN art programme have all made long-lasting connections 

and friendships. Their discussions revolved around creativity, playfulness, adventure and 

beauty, not business or the long-term plans of their respective organisations. In this 

sense, Arts@CERN both succumbs to and defies the larger CERN ideology. By 

recruiting artists who are fascinated by CERN to provide interpretations its work, we 

have seen how the organisation benefits in terms of PR. Yet, the scientists and artists 

who became part of Arts@CERN are meeting people they would perhaps not have

writes that her role as a non-scientist is “absolutely and completely crucial.”8 At the 

heart of its function, Arts@CERN remains a cultural project at the centre of a large

but this paradoxical existence may also be one of its strengths. While the project’s 

outcomes, as shown here, are not particularly diverse yet, the potential for the project to 

grow into a challenger of the status quo, exists. There are a number of different types of 

artists waiting for that opportunity: the hundreds of Collide@CERN applications is 

proof of this. As the programme expands, the scene is set for more artists gaining access 

in order to disrupt and examine CERN’s culture. 

Analysing the artists’ work and experiences at CERN can, as this thesis has 

shown, reveal how and why the organisation seeks to ‘sell science’ to the public. But if 

the art programme is left to CERN to interpret, the outcome will be PR-based, including 

scientifically correct contract art. CERN is an expensive and exclusive organisation of 

modern science, confident of its importance in the world. As former Director General 

Heuer put it, the Higgs boson ensured that CERN has “found the reason why we can 

physically exist.”9 The potential of the art programme lies in resurrecting the broader 

public debate about high-energy physics and the value of “big science”, rather than 

acting as free publicity for an arts patron. If the common notion implies that artists 

should exercise freedom of speech in their work, we cannot fail to comment on their role 

as contract artists producing politically and scientifically correct SciArt in large 

organisations. In a time when culture can be a commodity, art at CERN risks becoming 

an exercise in selling science. But when individual scientists and artists are free to 

explore the world together, at the edge of their known universes, boundaries can be 

broken. This thesis contributes to knowledge by showing how CERN utilises the arts as 

PR as part of its own image-making and branding strategy. This case study also lends 

itself to the broader study of SciArt. It reveals the genre’s institutional nature, and shows

INTRODUCTION 
CULTURAL POLICY FOR ENGAGING WITH THE ARTS

This is CERN’s first cultural policy for engaging with the arts. It was conceived as the foundation 

for Collide@CERN – the International Artists Residency programme. It became quickly apparent 

that if there is to be an International Arts Residency scheme, CERN crucially needed a Cultural 

Policy for Engaging with the Arts to provide the essential policy framework and foundations for 

the Collide@CERN arts residency initiative, as well as for all other high quality arts engagement 

and activities. 

CERN's first cultural policy for engaging with the arts is called Great Arts for Great Science. 

Both arts and science are ways of exploring the world we live in and our place in the universe. 

Science demonstrates its effectiveness through tests, equations and proof thus creating new 

knowledge and certainty, the arts demonstrates its impact through the senses, transporting 

people to see the world and relate to each other with a sense of wonder through the power of the 

imagination. 

WHY GREAT ARTS FOR GREAT SCIENCE? 

Called Great Arts for Great Science, CERN`s cultural policy creates for the first time the 

essential foundation and framework at CERN for expertise and knowledge of the arts to 

match CERN`s world renown for expertise and knowledge in science. 

Great Science deserves Great Art – with the same high standards of selection and quality 

control that are made to employ talented world-class scientists, engineers and 

technologists at CERN, being matched by CERN selecting equally talented, world-class, 

innovative artists. The policy will enable this with a key recommendation, building in the 

necessary expertise by setting up for the first time an independent Cultural Advisory Board 
for engaging with the Arts (CABA). 

By adopting Great Arts for Great Science, CERN can clearly demonstrate to the global 

cultural community that it is a cultural force – by engaging its great science with great arts. 

2

Camilla Mork Rostvik
278



“GREAT” 
IS DEFINED AS... 

Established Talent – World-class and recognized excellence, exceptionalism and ability. 

Emerging Talent – New talent that demonstrates exceptionalism, innovation, imagination and 

the ability to break the mould in their art forms to create the truly original and inspirational. 

Whilst in science, greatness is measured according to the absolutes of scientific proof and 

results, in the arts it is judged and assessed according to a combination of the experience and 

knowledge of the history of the different art forms demonstrated by experts - who include 

practitioners, curators, directors, producers, and critics. These are the kinds of people qualified to 

make valued critical judgments and choices about artists and their quality, their exceptionalism 

and their ability – thus ensuring Great Art for Great Science. 

PLEASE NOTE:

The term ‘artists’ is used generically to encompass people who work in the fields of dance, 

literature, theatre, film and television, digital arts, visual arts, architecture, design and music – the 

entire range of artistic activity as it is defined in the outside world.

THE FOUR MAIN STRATEGIES 
FOR GREAT ARTS FOR GREAT SCIENCE 

The following four strategies are essential for ensuring that the aims, values, and missions of 

Great Arts for Great Science are implemented in the Cultural Policy: 

STRATEGY ONE 

To create expert knowledge in the arts, in addition to that provided by an arts professional, by 

setting up the honorary Cultural Advisory Board for engaging with the Arts (CABA) that will include 

arts professionals at the highest level. 

STRATEGY TWO 

To create clear entry points for artists to visit CERN in which CERN adopts a system for dealing 

with unsolicited cultural proposals and artists enquiries, including visits, with a single point of 

contact, an arts professional, who has cultural expertise and knowledge to evaluate the requests. 

The arts professional works with the Cultural Advisory Board for Engaging with the Arts when 

major partnership proposals are made. The most obvious and clear entry point for artists will be 

the Collide@CERN Arts Residency Programme. 

STRATEGY THREE 

To instigate Collide@CERN the arts residency scheme to encourage dialogue and exchange 

between arts and science at the same level by selecting imaginative and extraordinary artists for 

their excellence to work alongside CERN scientists. 

STRATEGY FOUR 

To provide for the first time professional cultural expertise and advice to already existing 

homegrown arts activities at CERN – CinéGlobe, for example – to enable them to fulfill their 

cultural potential.

abstracts.value: This thesis explores the historical and contemporary practices of cultural engagement and management at the European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN). It considers the history of art at CERN, and the role of the artists who have engaged with the organisation. Furthermore, it traces CERN's history from the beginning of the organisation in 1954 to the contemporary art programme Arts@CERN, including the artist-in-residency competition Collide@CERN (both initiated in 2011). Approaching the topic from an interdisciplinary angle, the thesis utilises art history, science history, critical studies of branding and public relations, science communication and various theoretical disciplines in order to understand why selected artists are being invited to collaborate with CERN today. My original contribution to knowledge is a case study showing the institutional nature of SciArt (an art genre that combines art and science) at CERN, connecting this to the institutional use of art and artists as public relations.

titles.title: At the Edge of their Universe: Artists, Scientists and Outsiders at CERN

abstracts.value: Quantum batteries (QBs) represent a promising and emerging class of energy storage devices that exploit the principles of quantum mechanics to achieve superior performance compared to conventional, classical batteries. In this work, we investigate the charging dynamics of a QB in a bipartite system composed of two qubits, where one qubit acts as a charger and the other as the battery, each embedded in an independent cavity reservoir. The model incorporates multiphoton atom-cavity interactions as well as quenched disorder (QD) in the system-reservoir coupling, including discrete, uniform, Gaussian, and Cauchy-Lorentz distributions. The resulting dynamics are analyzed in both weak- and strong-coupling regimes. We examine how the multiphoton order affects the internal energies of the charger and the battery, and show that increasing the multiphoton order leads to enhanced dissipation and a reduction of the energy transferred to the battery. By comparing different disorder statistics, we find that uniform and discrete QDs can partially mitigate decoherence and yield higher charging efficiency compared to Gaussian and Cauchy-Lorentz QDs. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that strong system-reservoir coupling induces non-Markovian dynamics accompanied by rapid energy loss and suppression of ergotropy and efficiency. In contrast, efficient charging and partial revival features are predominantly observed in the weak-coupling, Markovian regime, where coherent dynamics are preserved.

titles.title: Impact of quenched disorder and multiphoton interaction on the dynamics of a quantum battery

abstracts.value: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.

titles.title: Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable

abstracts.value: For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error ($\varepsilon=0$), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every $0\le\varepsilon<1$, the $\varepsilon$-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.

abstracts.value: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.

titles.title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions

abstracts.value: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics, such as models that predict reconstructed jets from partons, are often evaluated on $1\text{D}$ marginal divergences among other metrics. Taken alone these metrics can reward conditional collapse. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network (MDN) on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model on two of the four. We instead score the models with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, taking the exact marginal as the reference. We show how global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, and we also report it within bins of a conditioning variable, where that dependence largely goes away. We then introduce a data-driven $k$-Nearest-Neighbor ($k$-NN) extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both models agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests that current architectures have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell.

titles.title: Estimating Spectrum-Free Information Bounds for Generative Surrogates Beyond Conditional Collapse

abstracts.value: A recent remarkable paper by OpenAI showed that the spin-one Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit. The proof elegantly deduces this gap from the Hamiltonian's spectrum on a finite system. This basic idea is an inequality involving the purity of the original Gibbs state and a dual Gibbs state that is defined via space-time rotation. Here we consider a few generalizations of this purity bootstrap argument. We first extend it to arbitrary spatial dimensions. Our main result uses the space-time duality between symmetry generators and symmetry twists to obtain upper bounds on the splitting of nearly degenerate low-energy states, together with a nonzero gap above them, from finite-system information. As applications, we show that finite-system calculations for the 2+1-D toric code in a field and the 2+1-D transverse-field Ising model establish parameter regimes with four and two low-lying states whose splittings are bounded from above by $e^{-cL}$ and $e^{-cL^2}$ respectively for arbitrarily large system size $L$, while the gap above these states remains nonzero in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we extend it to fermionic systems and use a finite calculation to establish a symmetric mass generation phase in a $2+1$-D fermionic model. Finally, we apply the bootstrap to tensor-network states and establish exponential decay of connected correlations of all local operators in the symmetric square-lattice spin-one state introduced by Jian and Zaletel.

titles.title: Extensions of the Haldane gap proof: higher dimensions, near degeneracy, fermions and tensor-network states

abstracts.value: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.

titles.title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection

abstracts.value: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.

abstracts.value: The cosmological principle may require more than observations demand: what is needed is isotropic expansion without vorticity. Extended Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (eFLRW) cosmologies realise this with a non-vanishing anisotropic spatial curvature that is balanced by an anisotropic stress while the shear vanishes. Thorsrud and others investigated such scenarios for free differential $p$-forms. Here we extend the analysis to non-Abelian $p$-forms ($p=0,\dots,4$) with self interactions. The balance requires the anisotropic stress to decay as $a^{-2}$, $a$ being the cosmological scale factor, which we combine with the gauge-field continuity equation. The general results indicate that, in the presence of a potential, fine-tuning of the same is needed in order to balance the curvature. Notably, this is not the case for a $3$-form field $\underline{H}^a$ with a potential term $V(\underline{H}^2)=A+B\,\underline{H}^2$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants: in Bianchi class A, an uncharged 3-form balances the curvature with this potential without any tuning, and a charged one does so for a suitably chosen connection. This is the only candidate we have found where the potential does not require tuning. It is also an interesting candidate as it can be interpreted as a cosmological constant in combination with a dark-matter sector mimicking curvature.

abstracts.value: Determining centrality of heavy-ion collisions with high resolution is essential for event-by-event analyses, in particular for net-proton fluctuation measurements aimed at locating the QCD critical point. Supervised machine-learning approaches rely on labels generated by model and therefore inherit the model dependence of the training target. In this work, we propose an unsupervised method to determine collision centrality based on optimal transport. Each collision is represented by its 1-Wasserstein distances to a fixed set of landmark events chosen to cover the measured multiplicity range. A point-cloud network trained by contrastive learning then compresses these distances into a compact event embedding, which is partitioned into equal-size centrality classes. We find that this approach groups events with similar $N_{\rm part}$ and yields a better centrality resolution, quantified by the normalized width of the $N_{\rm part}$ distribution, than the conventional method of cutting on particle multiplicity. The method, however, encounters a bottleneck once realistic kinematic cuts are applied to the particles. We attribute this degraded performance to the loss of distinct features between central and peripheral collisions because of applying kinematic cuts. The application of optimal transport to centrality determination in experimental data, remains an open problem that needs further study.

abstracts.value: We compute background corrections to the thermal free energy of free conformal field theories (CFTs) with a global abelian symmetry defined on a box with all sides infinitely long by turning on a flat gauge field in general dimensions. abstracts.value: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

abstracts.value: Pseudo-Dirac neutrinos are characterized by extremely small mass-squared differences between two nearly degenerate, strongly-mixed, active-sterile states. abstracts.value: We present a lattice formulation of N=1 supersymmetric QCD (SQCD) based on overlap fermions, providing a discretization consistent with the Ginsparg-Wilson relation. Particular emphasis is placed on the construction of Yukawa terms that preserve a lattice-modified chiral symmetry involving overlap quarks and gluinos. To realize this modified chiral symmetry in the Yukawa sector, we follow Lüscher's strategy and introduce auxiliary Dirac and Majorana fermionic fields for the quark and gluino fields, respectively. After functional integration over these auxiliary fields, ultralocal interaction terms arise as additional contributions to the lattice action. Within this framework, and using the Wilson gauge action for gluons, we also carry out one-loop perturbative calculations. In particular, we compute the self-energies of the quark, gluon, gluino, and squark fields in the presence of quark and squark masses, enabling an unambiguous determination of the corresponding field and mass counterterms on the lattice. This work provides a robust foundation for future perturbative determinations of the fine-tunings of the gauge, Yukawa, and quartic couplings, and already shows, as expected, a reduction in the number of required counterterms relative to Wilson-type fermions.

abstracts.value: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of $k$ copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls $β\|h\|_F\leβ_0$ of unknown Hamiltonian $h$, the single-copy rate is $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ for every fixed $β_0>0$, at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of $β_0$. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives $N>m^3/(8{,}553{,}600\,k\,ε^2)$ for blocks of at most $k$ copies and all $ε\le1/3600$; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of $\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, shows that the budget $mt^2$ behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether $1/k$ is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need $Ω(m^3/(ε^2\min\{\sqrt k,m\}))$ copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the $k$-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every $k$ on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. abstracts.value: Weak value (WV) describes the amplified response of a meter when the measured system undergoes postselection. abstracts.value: Is a supersymmetric bulk region with sub-200 GeV neutralinos and right-handed sleptons still feasible? Initially the bulk was the discovery target of the supersymmetry (SUSY) pioneers in the 1980s, though reality crashed those ambitions over the subsequent years and decades, presumptively excluding these light neutralinos and sleptons, inviting finely tuned dark matter scenarios to satisfy emerging high-precision relic density measurements. The answer to this important question is $yes$, if we consider the GUT model $\mathcal{F}$-$SU(5)$, namely, flipped $SU$(5) supplemented with a string derived TeV-scale extra $10+\overline{10}$ vector-like multiplet and charged vector-like singlet $(XE,XE^c)$, dubbed flippons. We pair $\mathcal{F}$-$SU(5)$ with effective supernatural supersymmetry (SUSY), known as generalized No-Scale Supergravity (SUGRA). This merging of $\mathcal{F}$-$SU(5)$ with generalized No-Scale SUGRA solves the SUSY electroweak fine-tuning problem and includes natural dark matter (NDM) that meets the latest 5$σ$ Planck satellite observations through annihilation only. The NDM in this model is imminently under test by the LUX-ZEPLIN 1000-day experiment, thus prospective observed events by LUX-ZEPLIN in 2026-27 will compel confirmation by the high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) energizing in 2030. Therefore, we present the parameter space observable at both LUX-ZEPLIN and the HL-LHC that is consistent with all presently operating experiments, including the LHC Run 3 gluino and squark constraints. Our results predict sub-200 GeV neutralinos and right-handed sleptons in the bulk that are not beyond detection, though more massive electroweakinos greater than 600 GeV are also allowed.

abstracts.value: The decomplexification procedure establishes a mathematical equivalence between finite dimensional quantum dynamics and classical dynamics by mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one. In this way, one can prepare the solution of classical differential equations to be implemented using quantum computation tools. In the present work, we recall the decomplexification procedure and also discuss several distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations, so as to obtain the corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.

abstracts.value: We present the first search for fixed-polarization dark photon (DP) dark matter in the 44-52$μ\mathrm{eV}$ mass range, corresponding to 10.7-12.5GHz. abstracts.value: Determining the entanglement Hamiltonian (EH) of an interacting quantum many-body system remains a fundamental challenge beyond special analytically tractable cases. Here we develop an observable-matching framework for learning effective EHs, which we demonstrate using response estimates from quantum Monte Carlo. As applications of this framework, we first calibrate the overall prefactor of the lattice Bisognano--Wichmann (LBW) construction using equal-time correlations and then learn spatially resolved couplings beyond its prescribed profile, without assuming a specific functional form for their spatial dependence. Trained solely on local correlations, the learned EHs reproduce benchmarked von Neumann and second Rényi entropies in $1$D and second Rényi entropies in $2$D. For a strong-bond cut associated with special surface criticality at the $(2+1)$D $O(3)$ Wilson--Fisher critical point, free-form learning outperforms the calibrated LBW ansatz in predicting the second Rényi entropy and reveals spatially nonuniform coupling renormalizations. Importantly, the learned EH also provides access to the von Neumann entropy in this setting, revealing a negative subleading correction and extending previous Rényi entropy findings to the von Neumann case. Directly evaluating the von Neumann entropy in such $(2+1)$D interacting quantum many-body systems remains challenging for conventional numerical methods. These results establish observable-based learning as a route to constructing effective entanglement Hamiltonians beyond prescribed spatial profiles in higher-dimensional interacting systems.

abstracts.value: Even a recovery that maximizes worst-input entanglement fidelity can retain avoidable errors in subsequent measurements. Entanglement fidelity is the probability of passing a test of whether the state and its entanglement were preserved; infidelity is the probability of failing it. Operational error is the largest possible change in any measurement probability, quantified by the normalized diamond distance. For every finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, we prove that operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity have the same minimum over all recovery operations. The proof constructs one final unitary (a reversible quantum operation) that makes any recovery's operational error no greater than its original worst-input entanglement infidelity. With a retained noise record, we determine the optimal error and characterize all optimal decoders subject to a Kraus-rank limit for each outcome. For a fixed decoded channel, a semidefinite program finds the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. We characterize all optimal final corrections and show that, at a fixed error floor $0<ε<1$, the operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size $s$ is at worst of order $s^{4/3}$, while the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity.

abstracts.value: In this work, we revisit the tidal Love numbers (TLNs) of several classes of exotic compact objects (ECOs) using the recently derived full perturbed junction conditions. We investigate four representative thin-shell models: wormholes, de Sitter gravastars with zero surface energy density, general de Sitter gravastars, and anti-de Sitter gravastars. Previous studies of wormholes and de Sitter gravastars with zero surface energy density, based on simplified matching conditions, suggested that the TLNs of ultracompact ECOs vanish logarithmically in the black-hole (BH) limit, leading to the conjecture that this logarithmic dependence is a generic feature of ultracompact exotic objects. We show that this logarithmic behavior is not universal once the full perturbed junction conditions are imposed. In particular, the odd-parity TLNs exhibit polynomial scaling in the BH limit for all the models considered, while the even-parity sector displays both logarithmic and polynomial behaviors depending on the model. We also find that the signs of the TLNs can differ qualitatively from previous results, especially in the odd-parity sector. Our results demonstrate that the tidal response of ECOs is strongly affected by the perturbed matching conditions and that the previously conjectured universal logarithmic scaling near the BH limit is not generic.

abstracts.value: Quantifying the interactivity of quantum instruments is fundamental to understanding their resource structure and operational capabilities. Here, we introduce the interactive weight of quantum instruments as a resource quantifier that measures the minimum fraction of an instrument that cannot be explained by non-interactive components. Through quantum-information tasks including quantum-state recovery, positive linear loss games, and environment-assisted input-blind extraction, we establish quantitative bounds on the interactive weight of quantum instruments and exact operational characterizations of its complementary quantity, the maximal non-interactive content. In particular, we extend environment-assisted input-blind extraction to the setting of restricted environmental access and develop a corresponding framework. Within the allowed-operations framework introduced by Hsieh et al., we establish fundamental resource-theoretic properties of the interactive weight of quantum instruments, including faithfulness, convexity, and monotonicity under deterministic allowed operations. Furthermore, we prove that the maximal non-interactive content satisfies exact multiplicativity under independent parallel composition, yielding necessary constraints on multicopy resource conversion and establishing the finite-copy maximal-weight distillation no-go result under deterministic allowed operations. These results establish a unified theoretical framework for the interactive weight of quantum instruments from the perspectives of resource quantification, operational interpretation, and resource conversion, providing systematic theoretical tools for the quantitative comparison and conversion of interactive quantum instruments.

abstracts.value: There is a rich class of bipartite quantum correlations between qubits which are consistent both with measurements performed in parallel and measurements performed in sequence. This phenomenon has recently been termed \emph{quantum causal confusion}, which is made mathematically precise by the notion of a dual state---a bipartite density operator whose associated correlations are causally ambiguous. A natural question is then whether or not the spatial and temporal scenarios associated with a dual state are fundamentally indistinguishable from a causal perspective. Here we show that as long as the reduced density operator of a dual state is oblique---meaning that all coefficients in its Pauli expansion are non-zero---then the underlying joint probabilities giving rise to such causally ambiguous correlations will differ in the spatial and temporal scenarios. Specifically, the temporal joint probabilities will inherently violate the no-signalling condition, thus eliminating quantum causal confusion. Moreover, as oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, the elimination of quantum causal confusion is the norm rather than an exception.

titles.title: Elimination of quantum causal confusion in the presence of dual states

abstracts.value: Binary millisecond pulsars (MSPs) serve as exceptional astrophysical laboratories for a wide range of astrophysical studies, all of which rely on precise property measurements allowed by pulsar timing. In this paper, we present high-precision timing solutions for seven binary MSPs monitored by the European Pulsar Timing Array. By combining data collected from the five largest radio telescopes in Europe, as well as their coherently combined form, the Large European Array for Pulsars, we achieve phase-coherent timing solutions for all seven pulsars. We conduct a Bayesian timing and noise analysis on the combined data, yielding measurements of astrometric and orbital parameters with broadly improved precision, some reported for the first time. For PSRs J0125-2327, J1741+1351 and J2043+1711, we determine their distances and transverse velocities from astrometric measurements, and infer their masses via Shapiro delay measurements. Additionally, we examine the various contributions to the secular orbital-period variations for PSRs J0125-2327, J1125+7819 and J1741+1351, and estimate their kinematic distances. For PSRs J0125-2327 and J1741+1351, we detect the signature of annual-orbital parallax in the timing data. This allows us to derive a strongly favored, unique solution for the orbital ascending node and inclination angle for PSR J0125-2327, and a tightly constrained ascending node for PSR J1741+1351. Moreover, we use the orbital periods and their derivatives for several binary MSPs to place upper limits on gravitational-wave strain in both the sub-nanohertz and microhertz frequency regimes. Our results show that the orbits of binary MSPs could provide stringent constraints in microhertz range, thereby possibly complementing standard pulsar-timing-array analyses in the future.

titles.title: High precision timing of seven binary millisecond pulsars with the European Pulsar Timing Array

abstracts.value: We construct a quantum action for heterotic string field theory that satisfies the quantum Batalin-Vilkovisky equation. Assuming a triangulation of the bosonic moduli space, the prescription for inserting picture-changing operators is determined based on a quantum L-infinity structure. After concretely constructing some of the lower-order interactions, we propose a general prescription, which generalizes that for constructing the classical interactions governed by a classical L-infinity structure. Assuming it does not suffer from spurious poles, all quantum interactions are determined by iteratively solving differential equations and transforming the solutions via IBL-infinity-transfer. To demonstrate the consistency of our prescription, we compute the one-loop two-point functions (modulo the spurious pole issue) and show that they agree with those in the first-quantized formulation.

titles.title: Quantum action for heterotic string field theory with quantum L-infinity structure

abstracts.value: Quench dynamics offer valuable insights to topological matter, wherein the emergent topological phenomena serve as a dynamic probe to the topology of static Hamiltonians. While such a practice has been widely applied to detect the Abelian band topology or the Euler-class topology of band nodes, little is known regarding the quench dynamics of non-Abelian topological insulators in multiband systems, where the intertwining geometry of all eigenstates necessitates the description of noncommutative topological charges. Here we propose a quench protocol for non-Abelian topological insulators, so that the underlying topology can be systematically probed using dynamic signatures. Specifically, we develop a band-projection scheme to extract the gap-resolved topology from dynamic skyrmions in the emergent quasimomentum--time manifolds of the quench processes. These skyrmions are characterized by a series of gap-resolved dynamic Chern numbers, which enable us to reconstruct the full non-Abelian topology of the post-quench Hamiltonian, including the global non-Abelian topological charge and edge-state patterns under the open-boundary condition. Our proposal offers dynamical access to non-Abelian topology in multiband systems, and can be readily implemented using photons or cold atoms.

titles.title: Probing Non-Abelian Topology through Quench Dynamics

abstracts.value: We present a systematic search for radio emission from cataclysmic variables (CVs) across four wide-field radio surveys in the 0.7-4 GHz frequency range: VLASS; RACS; VAST; and EMU. We generated a reliable catalog of 2225 optically-identified CV candidates using a multi-stage cross-match, combined with systematic and manual verification; 1374 are matched to Gaia sources within the radio surveys' footprints. Among these, we detected six CVs in at least one epoch (at 1e16.5-1e17.5 erg/s/Hz, consistent with the typical population of radio-detected CVs); five had been detected in radio before. IX Vel, the closest nova-like CV, is detected in radio for the first time and shows quasi-persistent low-level emission across a 10 hr EMU (943.5 MHz) observation. Given most epochs detected no CV, we stacked images without radio detections to better constrain time-averaged brightnesses. We created co-added images and placed upper limits on low-level radio emission from each of the 423 individual CVs within the VAST footprint. To constrain the median brightness for the entire CV population, we combined all Gaia-matched CVs in each survey into single population-wide stacked images, detecting no statistically significant emission. Finally, we created population-wide image stacks of the CVs within 100 pc, using 14 epochs from 5 CVs in EMU to constrain their median persistent specific luminosity to <3e14 erg/s/Hz.

titles.title: Systematic Search for Cataclysmic Variables in Radio Surveys: First Radio Detection of IX Velorum

abstracts.value: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $Ω_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $Ω_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.

titles.title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate

abstracts.value: Detecting single gravitons is possible through the extraction of discrete energy quanta from passing gravitational waves. For decades, this was considered hopeless, with estimates suggesting a detector the size of Jupiter. Here, I explain how these earlier estimates relied on the highly inefficient electron ionization process, while the absorption through the full mass quadrupole of a macroscopic system can bring graviton detection within experimental reach. Operating in the LIGO frequency band solves the challenges of graviton sources and noise suppression, allowing gravitons to be extracted from known passing gravitational waves and detection events to be heralded by classical gravitational-wave observations. Combined with the ability to resolve single energy quanta in macroscopic systems, such as in quantum acoustics, this opens a realistic path toward graviton detection. I also discuss the general limitations of particle detection in establishing an underlying quantum theory, illustrated by an energy-nonconserving semiclassical alternative. Nevertheless, the semiclassical alternative is not standard classical wave physics, and extracting $E=\hbarω$ from a passing wave constitutes bona fide particle detection. This opens the way not only to the first detection of individual gravitons, but also to experimentally probing linearized quantum gravity and the graviton counting statistics of gravitational waves.

titles.title: Demystifying Graviton Detection

abstracts.value: Post-common-envelope evolution (CEE) circumbinary disks (CBDs) form when part of the ejected envelope remains bound and circularizes around the stripped core and its companion. Leveraging results of scale-free hydrodynamical simulations, we develop a framework to model the effect of such disks on subsequent binary evolution, and implement it in the population synthesis code COMPAS. Applying our framework to double neutron star (DNS) merger progenitors, we find that CBDs generally induce substantial orbital shrinkage, changing the merging DNS population and lowering the overall merger rate. We explore an extensive grid of binary-evolution and disk models, and find that CBD interactions reduce the DNS merger rate by up to $28\%$, primarily through 'premature' mergers between the neutron star (NS) and the giant's core. These mergers may power luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs), occurring at a fiducial rate of $\simeq11 \:\rm Gpc^{-3} \rm yr^{-1}$. Our results indicate that natal kicks contribute little to LFBOT offsets, and that they should be associated with young stellar populations, though not necessarily active star-forming regions. Since LFBOT progenitors would otherwise produce short-delay DNS mergers, CBDs further challenge DNS mergers as the source of early r-process enrichment. For surviving DNS mergers, accretion from the disk leads to higher chirp masses, potentially explaining the puzzling mass of GW190425. Our framework provides a general tool for studying CBD-binary interactions in post-CEE systems.

titles.title: Double Neutron Star Mergers and Fast Blue Optical Transients: A Circumbinary Disk Connection

abstracts.value: We examine the field produced by a stationary current loop encircling a static Bocharova--Bronnikov--Melnikov--Bekenstein (BBMB) black hole and the response of charged test particles. From the dipole projection of Maxwell's equations, we obtain closed-form interior and exterior radial functions, and we test them against a multipole expansion of the localized source whose radial functions are also elementary. Every horizon-regular mode vanishes at the degenerate horizon $r_+=M$, so the magnetic flux through the horizon is zero. For a loop at $r_0=10M$, the dipole errors in the equatorial potential and polar field remain below $10\%$ for $r\lesssim0.42\,r_0$ and $r\gtrsim3.02\,r_0$, but reach about $40\%$ and $80\%$ close to the loop. Using the resulting potential, we study the effective potential, circular orbits, the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), a binding-energy proxy, and epicyclic frequencies. Because the dipole field reverses its equatorial direction across the loop, a positive magnetic coupling $\mathcal{B}$ acts oppositely on the two sides. Above $\mathcal{B}_c\simeq0.0119$, the prograde radially stable orbits split into two bands separated by an unstable gap. At $\mathcal{B}=0.2$, the ISCO moves from $4M$ to $2.97M$, the exterior band begins at $45.46M$, and the ISCO binding-energy proxy grows from $8.14\%$ to $23.39\%$, compared with $5.72\%$ for neutral particles around a Schwarzschild black hole. For negative coupling, exterior orbits can be radially stable but vertically unstable. Higher multipoles preserve the large-coupling trends but shift the near-loop values appreciably, so the near-loop results apply to the projected source rather than to a thin ring.

titles.title: Circular motion and fundamental frequencies of charged particles in dipole magnetic field around magnetized Bocharova--Bronnikov--Melnikov--Bekenstein black holes

abstracts.value: We present a self-contained coordinate-matrix formulation of General Relativity in the harmonic gauge, providing a compact, index-free representation of the gravitational field equations within the algebra of $4\times 4$ real matrices $M_4$. By defining musical isomorphism operators ($\sharp, \flat$), metric adjoints ($\dagger$), and matrix-valued derivative vectors ($\bm{\mathcal{B}}, \bm{\mathcal{C}}, \bm{\mathcal{D}}^\sharp$), the Ricci tensor is recast into an algebraic matrix structure dominated by the Laplace--Beltrami operator $\Box_{\mathrm{LB}} \coloneqq \operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{G}^\sharp \partial^2)$, where $\partial^2 \coloneqq \bm{\partial}\bm{\partial}^T$ represents the matrix Hessian operator of second partial derivatives. Within this setting, Einstein's field equations naturally take the form of a non-linear wave equation for the metric matrix $\mathcal{G}$, giving rise to an index-free matrix representation of the gravitational energy-momentum pseudotensor $\bar{\mathcal{T}}$. We derive the explicit algebraic relation connecting $\bar{\mathcal{T}}$ with the classical Landau--Lifshitz energy-momentum complex $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{LL}}$, and express the associated local conservation law in a simple matrix divergence form, $\bm{\partial}^T \left((-g)(\mathcal{T}^{\sharp} + \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{LL}}^{\sharp})\right) = \bm{0}^T$. Finally, we illustrate the scope and applicability of the matrix formalism through three physical applications: weak-field linearized gravity, the exact derivation of Friedmann cosmological dynamics in harmonic time, and the complete formulation of linear scalar cosmological perturbations in both the Newtonian and harmonic gauges.

titles.title: Algebraic representation of General Relativity in harmonic gauge

abstracts.value: A coupling of photons to the cosmic neutrino asymmetry current has been proposed to explain the hinted isotropic rotation of CMB polarization. Gauge invariant UV completions require a Kalb-Ramond field that is exactly dual to a massless axion. We show that, in this case, the product of the axion-photon coupling and the axion-neutrino current coupling is fixed by the signal, $g_{aγ}/f_\ell=1/Λ_*^2$ with $Λ_*\simeq10$ TeV. Using $SU(2)_L$ gauge invariance we show that the dual axion couples to electrons as $g_{aγ}g_{ae}=m_e/Λ_*^2\simeq5\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. This value is excluded by the measured electron magnetic moment combined with light-shining-through-a-wall searches, as well as by stellar evolution. Conserved anomaly-free currents may evade these bounds, but then either a contact interaction among SM fermions excludes the model, or the relic neutrinos decouple from the signal. We conclude that cosmic neutrinos cannot induce a birefringence signal.

titles.title: Can cosmic neutrinos induce a cosmic birefringence signal?

abstracts.value: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-$1/2$ examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.

titles.title: Optimal quantum metrology with restricted controls
